\caption{One instance of \textsc{Screen}, the same model and the same site, run with and without the two tools; everything else identical. \emph{Left}: four distinct treatments over two rounds, rank 4/7\,---\,deficient over the six factors --- a design that cannot separate the main effects it was commissioned to separate. \emph{Right}: the agent adopts the supplied screening design, reaching 11 distinct treatments and full rank, so the six main effects become estimable and the design scores better on $c$. It then answers $6.0\times$ worse. The boxed rows are why: after round~2 the agent's stated recommendation is the inference tool's proposed point to six digits, and carries that tool's regret of $0.2066$. In the final turn it abandons the tool for its best observed treatment, recovering to $0.1723$ --- still worse than it managed with no tool at all. A better design and a worse answer are not a contradiction here: full rank makes the main effects estimable, but 12 points over six factors is close to one level a factor, and the same routine is handed twice as many when it chooses its own design (\S\ref{sec:results:findings}). This episode is not exceptional: of the 400 instances run both ways, the tooled arm submits the strictly wider design in 238 and, in 143 of those, also the worse answer. We show this one because the copying is exact. Table~\ref{tab:tools} aggregates the effect over all $20$ model--task pairs.}
\label{fig:transcript}
